dossier.topic: Kite-and-dart Penrose tiling grown by two substitution rules whose kite-to-dart count locks to the golden ratio
dossier.summary: Penrose kite-and-dart tilings grow from substitution rules. Each kite splits into two kites and two half-darts, and each dart splits into one kite and two half-darts. The result never repeats, yet the ratio of kites to darts settles to the golden ratio, so the tile count grows by a fixed factor of about 2.618 per generation.

facts.claim: A kite is a quadrilateral with interior angles 72, 72, 72 and 144 degrees. A dart is a non-convex quadrilateral with interior angles 36, 72, 36 and 216 degrees.

Penrose tiling features follow from a hierarchical pentagonal structure given by substitution rules: a kite decomposes into two kites and two half-darts, and a dart decomposes into one kite and two half-darts.
The ratio of the number of kites to darts in any sufficiently large P2 Penrose tiling approximates the golden ratio.
Inflating the kites and darts eventually makes them larger than the period parallelogram itself. This inflation property proves that any tiling of this kind is non-periodic.

The Bielefeld page for its two-prototile rhomb substitution gives the inflation factor as the golden mean, 1.618033988, and says all entries in powers of its substitution matrix are Fibonacci numbers.

visualisable_mechanisms.name: two-kite split
visualisable_mechanisms.description: Each kite is replaced by two smaller kites and two half-dart wedges; each dart is replaced by one smaller kite and two half-dart wedges. Cause: the substitution rule applied to every tile at once, so the whole patch is rewritten at each generation.
visualisable_mechanisms.render_or_sonify_hint: Start from one seed kite. On each step, every tile is replaced by its scaled-down pieces, drawn as nested pentagonal clusters with kites in one colour and darts in a second colour.

visualisable_mechanisms.name: kite-dart count lock
visualisable_mechanisms.description: Counts follow K' = 2K + D and D' = K + D, a derived consequence of the split rules (two half-darts reassemble into one dart). The eigenvector of that matrix gives a kite-to-dart ratio of phi to 1, so the ratio converges regardless of the seed.
visualisable_mechanisms.render_or_sonify_hint: Show a two-bar counter of kites and darts per generation. Early bars jump around, then the proportion settles to about 1.618 to 1 and stays there.

visualisable_mechanisms.name: generation shell growth
visualisable_mechanisms.description: The tile count is multiplied by the matrix eigenvalue phi squared, about 2.618, at each generation. Each new generation forms a shell around the earlier patch, so the piece builds up in layers over time.
visualisable_mechanisms.render_or_sonify_hint: Over a 20 second loop, reveal successive rings of smaller tiles around the seed, each ring holding about 2.6 times as many tiles as the one before, with the older rings fading but still visible.

visualisable_mechanisms.name: period-escape test
visualisable_mechanisms.description: Because inflated tiles eventually exceed any period parallelogram, no translated copy of the tiling can line up with itself exactly. Cause: the scale factor compounds faster than any fixed translation.
visualisable_mechanisms.render_or_sonify_hint: Overlay a shifted copy of the tiling in a thin outline. At each generation it visibly fails to match, and matching flashes only where a short patch happens to recur.

open_questions: The count matrix K' = 2K + D, D' = K + D is derived from the split rules and must be checked against a generated patch before the build relies on it.
Sources label the pieces differently (Robinson triangles versus half-darts), so the build needs one canonical decomposition for its code.
Does a single seed kite or dart fix one tiling under inflation, or does the choice of seed branch the result?

surprise.justification: A generalist expects a pattern built by repetition or a random-looking fill. In fact two fixed tile splits give an endless tiling that never repeats, and its kite-to-dart count locks to the golden ratio.

brief.title: Penrose kite and dart shells
brief.concept: A seed kite in a Penrose tiling is rewritten by two substitution rules at every generation, so ochre kites and rust darts grow outward in shells while their count settles toward the golden ratio.

mechanism_embodied.how_visualised: Every ochre kite is replaced by two smaller kites and two rust half-darts, and every dart by one kite and two half-darts, applied to all tiles at once each generation. The single seed kite at centre is the only starting tile. Each generation appears as a ring of smaller tiles around the older patch, and two bars in a corner show the kite and dart counts over time.

brief.discarded_obvious_idea: Obvious: a random-looking tiling filled by noise, with colours drifting across it. Rejected: the noise fill hides the substitution rule and the count lock, and it breaks the seeded-PRNG rule.
brief.motion_sound_plan: Mood applied: high tempo with dense fields and 4 cuts (never closer than 0.34 s), warm-consonant palette with mirrored radial symmetry, assertive framing with the patch filling the frame and a strong push-in then pull-back, experimental risk on the substitution tiling. No audio. Constraint: none.

storyboard.description: Ochre seed kite centred on a cream ground, mirrored about its long axis. By 2 s it has split into four pieces, two kites and two rust half-darts, forming a compact pentagonal cluster in the centre third of the frame.

Every tile is rewritten at once: kites split and darts split into a kite and two half-darts. Rings of smaller graphite-edged tiles spread outward from the centre, and the seed cluster fades to amber. The 8 s frame shows the patch filling the frame from centre to edge.

Peak: the camera pushes in on the newest shell, with many rings of tiny amber and rust tiles around a dense centre. Two bars in the top-left corner show kite and dart counts trading shares. Hard cuts between generations, each at least 0.34 s apart.

The camera pulls back to show the whole patch. Each outer shell holds more tiles than the shell inside it, and older shells fade to pale ochre but stay visible. The two corner bars rest near a 1.6 to 1 ratio, and the framing keeps beat 3's dense centre.

brief.memorable_moment: A seed kite splitting into four pieces, then rings of smaller ochre and rust tiles spreading outward from the centre.
brief.self_declared_risk: The substitution rule may be coded with a wrong decomposition, leaving overlaps or gaps, and the corner bars may not match the generated patch. The frame budget may also run out at the third generation.
brief.liner_note: The Penrose tiling entry on Wikipedia says a kite splits into two kites and two half-darts, and that in any sufficiently large P2 tiling the ratio of kites to darts approximates the golden ratio. The rule rewrites every tile at once, so each generation builds a larger patch around the older one, and the pattern is non-periodic. On screen, ochre kites and rust darts split into smaller pentagonal clusters, and each generation forms a new shell around the last. By the final beat the frame pulls back to show the whole patch, with the newest shell brightest.
